title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
directAnswer: Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (elements need not be contiguous). The classic DP is O(n²): dp[i] = longest LIS ending at i. The optimal is patience sorting with binary search — maintain a 'tails' array where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1, and binary-search each number into it: O(n log n) time.

rules: `tails[k]` = the **smallest possible tail** of an increasing subsequence of length `k+1`; the array stays sorted, so binary search applies.
For **strictly** increasing, binary-search with `lower_bound` / `bisect_left` (replace the first element `≥ x`); for non-decreasing use `upper_bound` / `bisect_right`.
`tails` is **not** a real subsequence — its *length* is the answer, but its contents may never co-occur in nums.
If `x` is larger than every tail, **append** (LIS grew); otherwise **overwrite** the first tail `≥ x` (keeps future options open).
The O(n²) DP (`dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j] for j<i, nums[j]<nums[i])`) is the fallback when you also need to *reconstruct* the subsequence.
whenToUse: Longest subsequence (non-contiguous) that is monotonic under some order
Can reduce 'best chain' problems (envelopes, pairs, box stacking) to an LIS after sorting
n is large enough that O(n²) is too slow → patience + binary search
Only the LENGTH is needed (binary-search version doesn't reconstruct)
antiSignals: Contiguous required → that's a subarray problem (Kadane-style), not subsequence
Need the actual subsequence, not just length → use O(n²) DP with parent pointers
Longest common subsequence of two arrays → 2-D DP, different recurrence
Counting the number of LIS → DP carrying both length and count
remember.takeaway: LIS has two canonical answers and you should know both: the O(n²) dp-ending-here DP (intuitive, reconstructable) and the O(n log n) patience-sorting trick (tails[] + binary search). The patience insight — keep the smallest tail per length to leave the most room — recurs across many 'longest chain' problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can write the standard O(n²) LIS DP cleanly, and whether you know the O(n log n) patience-sorting / binary-search optimization and can explain why the tails array stays sorted.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Confusing subsequence with subarray (requiring contiguity), or in the binary-search version using the wrong bound (bisect_right vs bisect_left) so 'strictly increasing' silently becomes 'non-decreasing'.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive the O(n²) DP, then explain the patience-sorting model: tails[k] is the minimal tail of a length-(k+1) subsequence, so a smaller tail always dominates — that's why binary search and overwrite are correct.

problemStatement:
Given an integer array `nums`, return **the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence**.

A **subsequence** is a sequence derivable from the array by deleting some or no elements **without changing the order** of the remaining elements. For example, `[3, 6, 2, 7]` is a subsequence of `[0, 3, 1, 6, 2, 2, 7]`.

The subsequence must be **strictly** increasing — equal adjacent values do not count.
constraints: The subsequence need NOT be contiguous (it's a subsequence, not a subarray)
Increasing means strictly increasing — duplicates cannot both be included
understanding: Pick elements left to right, skipping any you like, so that the values you keep strictly increase — maximize how many you keep. Order is preserved, gaps are allowed. 'Strictly' means [2, 2] counts as length 1, not 2.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Subsequence or subarray?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Subsequence — non-contiguous, order preserved. A subarray (contiguous) would be a completely different, easier problem.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Strictly increasing or non-decreasing?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Strictly. [1, 3, 3, 4] has an LIS of 3 ([1, 3, 4]), not 4. In the binary-search version this decides bisect_left vs bisect_right.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return the length or the actual subsequence?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The length. If they want the subsequence too, I'd use the O(n²) DP with parent pointers, since the patience array doesn't reconstruct directly.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large is n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 2500, so O(n²) (~6 million ops) passes. But I'll mention O(n log n) since interviewers usually want it, and it scales to much larger n.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Both correct; choose by what you need. Reconstruction → O(n²) DP. Just the length, large n → patience + binary search.

approaches.name: Dynamic Programming — dp Ending at i (O(n²))
approaches.whenToMention: The natural first DP. Lead here to show the recurrence cleanly, then optimize to O(n log n).
hints: Define dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence that ENDS exactly at index i. What does dp[i] depend on?
To end at i, the previous element must be some j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]. So dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over all such j (or 1 if none).
Two nested loops: outer i, inner j < i. Answer is the max over all dp[i], since the LIS can end anywhere.
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each i we scan all j < i → n + (n−1) + … ≈ n²/2 = O(n²) time. The dp array is O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Let `dp[i]` be the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence that *ends at index i*. Every element starts as its own length-1 subsequence; extend it by looking back at every earlier element smaller than `nums[i]`.

**Why anchor the subproblem on 'ending at i'.** The total LIS can end anywhere, which is hard to recurse on directly. Pinning the subproblem to 'ends exactly at i' makes the recurrence local and clean: any increasing subsequence ending at `i` is some shorter increasing subsequence ending at an earlier `j` (with `nums[j] < nums[i]`) plus `nums[i]` itself. So `dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j] for j < i where nums[j] < nums[i])`, defaulting to 1 when no smaller predecessor exists. The final answer is `max(dp)` because we don't know in advance which index the best subsequence ends on.

**Why strictness lives in the comparison.** The single condition `nums[j] < nums[i]` (strict `<`, not `<=`) is what enforces strictly increasing. Relax it to `<=` and `[7, 7, 7, 7]` would report 4 instead of 1. This one operator is the entire difference between the two problem variants.

**Why this is the version to reach for when you need the subsequence itself.** Because `dp[i]` records *where* each subsequence ends, you can store a `parent[i]` pointer to the `j` that produced the max and walk it backward to reconstruct the actual LIS. The faster patience-sorting method gives you only the length cleanly. State the O(n²) DP first; for n ≤ 2500 it even passes outright.
approaches.insight: The trick is choosing a subproblem you *can* recurse on: 'LIS ending at i' is local and composable, whereas 'LIS of the whole array' is not. Whenever the global objective is hard to break down, try anchoring it to 'ending at / using element i' — it's the workhorse framing for subsequence DPs.

diagrams.caption: Each dp[i] looks back at smaller earlier elements; dp[5]=3 comes from chaining 2→5→7.

edgeCases.behavior: No j satisfies nums[j] < nums[i] (all equal), so every dp[i] stays 1 → answer 1. Strict < is doing the work.

pitfalls: Using <= instead of < — turns strictly increasing into non-decreasing.
Returning dp[n-1] instead of max(dp) — the LIS need not end at the last index.
Forgetting to initialize dp to 1 — a lone element is already length 1.

approaches.name: Patience Sorting — tails[] + Binary Search (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Pitch it as 'keep the smallest possible tail for each subsequence length and binary-search each number in'.
hints: The O(n²) DP rescans all earlier elements each step. What if you kept a compact summary that lets you place each new number with a binary search instead?
Maintain tails[], where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail value of any increasing subsequence of length k+1. This array is always sorted.
For each x, binary-search the first tail >= x. If none, append x (LIS grew). Otherwise overwrite that tail with x. The answer is len(tails).
approaches.complexityReasoning: n elements, each placed with an O(log n) binary search into tails → O(n log n) time. tails holds at most n values → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain an array `tails` where `tails[k]` is the *smallest possible tail* of any strictly increasing subsequence of length `k+1`. Process each number with a binary search; the final length of `tails` is the LIS length.

**Why a smaller tail always dominates.** Suppose two increasing subsequences both have length 3, ending in 9 and in 5. The one ending in 5 is strictly better for the future: anything that could extend the 9-ending one can also extend the 5-ending one (since 5 < 9 leaves more room), but not vice versa. So for each length we only ever need to remember the *minimum* achievable tail — that's exactly `tails[k]`. Keeping the minimum is what lets us throw away dominated states and collapse the DP.

**Why tails stays sorted (so binary search is valid).** A longer increasing subsequence must end on a larger value than the increasing subsequence one shorter that it extends, so `tails` is strictly increasing by construction. That sortedness is what licenses the `O(log n)` binary search — we're searching a sorted array every step.

**The placement rule, and the strict-vs-non-strict knob.** For each `x`, binary-search for the leftmost tail that is `≥ x` (`bisect_left` / `lower_bound`). If `x` exceeds every tail, it extends the longest subsequence so we **append** it. Otherwise we **overwrite** that first `≥ x` tail with `x` — same length, but now a smaller (better) tail. Using `lower_bound` (replace first `≥ x`) gives *strictly* increasing; switching to `upper_bound` (first `> x`) would allow equal values and solve the non-decreasing variant. That single choice is the entire difference.

**The crucial caveat.** `tails` is **not** a valid subsequence of `nums` — its contents can be a mix of values that never appeared together in order. Only its *length* is meaningful. If the interviewer wants the actual subsequence, fall back to the O(n²) DP with parent pointers (or augment patience sorting with index bookkeeping). Say this explicitly; it's a favorite follow-up.
approaches.insight: The leap is realizing that for each subsequence length, only the smallest tail matters — every larger tail is dominated and can be discarded. That reduces an O(n²) 'compare against all predecessors' to an O(log n) 'binary-search into a sorted summary'. The dominance-pruning idea (keep only the non-dominated frontier) is a reusable optimization far beyond LIS.

x is larger than all tails → it extends the longest subsequence.

diagrams.title: tails[] evolving on [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18]
diagrams.caption: Overwrites keep each length's tail as small as possible; appends grow the LIS. Final length is the answer.

edgeCases.behavior: Each 7 finds the first tail >= 7 at index 0 and overwrites it; tails stays [7], length 1. bisect_left enforces strictness.
tails: [1] → [1,3] → overwrite 3 with 2 → [1,2]. Length 2. Shows overwrite doesn't lose the answer even though [1,2] isn't the literal LIS [1,3].

pitfalls: Using bisect_right / upper_bound — silently solves non-decreasing, wrong on [7,7,7].
Treating tails as the actual subsequence — only its length is meaningful.
Appending when you should overwrite (or vice versa) — append only when x exceeds every tail (index == size).

commonMistakes: Solving for a contiguous subarray instead of a (non-contiguous) subsequence.
Using <= so the result is non-decreasing instead of strictly increasing.
Believing the patience-sorting tails[] array IS the longest increasing subsequence — only its length is correct.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Subarray vs subsequence
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A subsequence allows gaps; a subarray must be contiguous. Requiring contiguity reports a far shorter answer — e.g. [0,1,0,3,2,3] gives 2 (contiguous) instead of 4.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong binary-search bound
commonMistakesDetailed.why: bisect_right (upper_bound) lets equal values append, turning strict LIS into non-decreasing. [7,7,7,7] would wrongly return 4.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: i = bisect.bisect_right(tails, x)   # allows equal values
commonMistakesDetailed.good: i = bisect.bisect_left(tails, x)    # first tail >= x → strictly increasing

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Reading the subsequence off tails[]
commonMistakesDetailed.why: tails holds the minimal tail per length, not actual chained elements. Its contents may never co-occur in order; only len(tails) is the answer.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return tails; // NOT a valid subsequence
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return size; // only the LENGTH is meaningful

followupVariations.title: Russian Doll Envelopes
followupVariations.hint: Sort by width asc, height desc on ties, then run LIS on heights — reduces 2-D nesting to 1-D LIS.

followupVariations.title: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequence
followupVariations.hint: Carry both length and count per index in the O(n²) DP; combine counts when lengths tie.

followupVariations.title: Maximum Length of Pair Chain
followupVariations.hint: Sort by second element and greedily chain — an LIS-flavored chaining problem.

followupVariations.title: Longest Common Subsequence
followupVariations.hint: Different shape — 2-D DP over two strings; LIS reduces to LCS against a sorted copy in some variants.

patternNote: Patience Sorting / LIS. Many 'longest chain under an order' problems (envelopes, pair chains, box stacking) reduce to LIS after a clever sort. Know the O(n²) DP for reconstruction and the O(n log n) tails+binary-search for length; the dominance-pruning idea generalizes widely.
